title: Five pillars: accuracy, vocabulary and sentences

tips.title: Hunt your own spelling mistakes
tips.body: Make a list of the 10 words you yourself misspell again and again, and in the last 2–3 minutes of the exam look for just those. Small slips (teh / recieve) do little harm, but a spelling mistake that changes the meaning (advice / advise, then / than, lose / loose) is treated as using the wrong word — far more serious.

tips.title: Fix the five basic grammar errors first
tips.body: Tense, subject–verb agreement, singular/plural, adjective/adverb and unclear pronouns tell the examiner your foundation is weak (The number of cars has increased; Sales rose significantly). Fix these five before thinking about "advanced" grammar: 15 simple but correct sentences get a higher band than 10 complex sentences with 6 mistakes.

tips.title: Upgrade words only when you are sure
tips.body: Replace a common word with a more precise one only if you are sure it is correct (a big problem → a serious / significant problem), because an uncommon word used wrongly loses more marks than a common word used correctly. To avoid repeating words, write two synonyms for each key noun of the question on the question paper before you start (children → young people, minors).

tips.title: A correct simple sentence always wins
tips.body: Mix simple, compound and complex sentences — roughly one complex sentence after every two simple/compound ones. Golden rule: if you are not sure, break the long sentence into two short ones and join them with a linking word. Never use a double connector: not "Although it was raining, but we went out".

tips.title: Write active; use passive only when needed
tips.body: The passive does not make writing "academic" — the active voice is direct, clear and strong (My friends have supported the decision). Use the passive only when the doer is unimportant, unknown or deliberately hidden, for a polite suggestion, or to describe a process, as in a Task 1 flow chart (The beans are roasted, then ground).

title: Coherence and linking words: make your writing flow

tips.title: One paragraph, one topic sentence
tips.body: Start every paragraph with a specific topic sentence ("People move to cities for three main reasons.", not the vague "Many people move to cities.") and make every other sentence support it. To check, cover everything except the topic sentence and ask of each sentence: "Does this support the topic sentence?" If not, cut it or move it — drifting away from the topic is a very costly mistake.

tips.title: Keep paragraphs a readable size
tips.body: Long paragraphs tire the reader: 80–150 words (roughly 5–8 lines) is ideal, and beyond 200 words the reader loses the thread. A one-sentence emphatic paragraph can be used very rarely — never in Task 1.

tips.title: One connective every two or three sentences
tips.body: Connectives such as First, However, As a result and For example tell the reader what kind of sentence comes next, and IELTS gives marks for this directly. But if every sentence starts with one, the writing sounds mechanical and gets stuck at band 6. Pick 2–3 words from each function and use them until they feel natural.

tips.title: Match the connective to the logic
tips.body: Moreover before an opposing point, or As a result before something that is not a result, shows the examiner you do not understand the word. A connective at the start of a sentence takes a comma (However, …), while whereas / while / although join two clauses inside one sentence.

tips.title: Phrases to drop for good
tips.body: Never write "According to me" — write In my view / In my opinion / I believe. Do not use "At last" (it means after a long wait), and do not start a conclusion with "Last but not least". On the contrary does not mean on the other hand; use it only to reject a mistaken idea: He is not lazy; on the contrary, he works twelve hours a day.

title: Task 1: 5 red lines that cost bands

tips.title: 150 is the floor, about 180 the target
tips.body: Never write fewer than 150 words — even 148 loses marks — and don't go above 200, or not more than 20 minutes: more words mean more mistakes and less time for Task 2, which carries double the weight. Don't count in the exam hall; find out beforehand how many lines 170 words take in your handwriting (usually 12–14).

tips.title: Overview goes second, with no numbers
tips.body: Write four paragraphs: introduction, overview, and two body paragraphs with numbers. Put the overview (the 2–3 biggest features, without numbers) right after the introduction — if it is left for the end and you run out of time, a whole band is lost in Task Achievement. A conclusion is optional, and if you write one it is a summary, never an opinion.

tips.title: No opinion, no I, we, you
tips.body: Task 1 only tests whether you can describe the given data, so any opinion, advice or explanation of why something happened ("probably because of the pandemic") lowers Task Achievement. The report is impersonal: write The chart shows…, never We can see… or You can notice….

tips.title: Understand the graph before you write
tips.body: Read the title, both axis labels, the unit and the legend, and ask: what is measured, in which unit, over what period, how many categories? Start writing only when you can explain it to yourself in one sentence — otherwise you end up describing the wrong thing. Spend about the first 3 minutes on this.

tips.title: Match the tense to the time
tips.body: The first sentence (The graph shows…) is always present. Past years → past tense (Sales rose in 2010); no year → present; future years → not will but is expected / projected / forecast to + verb (Solar output is expected to triple by 2030). Process and diagram → present simple, usually passive.

title: Task 1: overview, trends and comparisons

tips.title: Build the overview from the big picture
tips.body: The overview gives the 2–3 biggest points without numbers: the overall direction (increased / decreased / fluctuated), the highest and lowest, the position at the end compared with the start, any major exception (a big slump, a crossover), and with several lines who is at the top and bottom at the end. For a map, it is the overall character of the change — including what stayed the same.

tips.title: Select and group — no data dump
tips.body: Pick 4–6 key points (start, end, peak, trough, crossover, biggest change), not every number. Arrange the data by behaviour — the big ones, the small ones, the ones that changed, and the exception — not left to right or row by row. Express numbers as relationships where possible: nearly doubled, a third, almost level with.

tips.title: One trend sentence, one clear formula
tips.body: Use Subject + verb + adverb + time + amount: Visitor numbers + rose + sharply + between 1995 and 2005 + to 480,000. Every trend sentence needs direction, degree, number and time, and no verb, adverb or connective should appear three times. Check your prepositions: by / to / at / from…to.

tips.title: No rise or fall without time
tips.body: Bars of categories and a single pie do not "rise" or "fall" — write X is higher than Y, X has the largest share, accounts for. A pie does not grow; the share of a segment does. From 25% to 40% is a rise of 15 percentage points, not 15 percent, and several pies are compared segment by segment.

tips.title: Processes and maps: follow the arrows
tips.body: In a process, describe by following the arrows in the present simple (man-made → passive), vary the sequencers instead of "Then… Then…", and add nothing that is not in the diagram. In a map, compare the changes rather than writing two inventories, give compass directions, and use past for a past map and will be built for a plan.

tips.title: 260–290 words in 40 minutes
tips.body: Never go below 250 words (even 248 is a penalty), and above 320 there is no gain — mistakes simply increase. Spend 0–5 minutes reading, deciding the type, brainstorming and planning, 5–35 writing and 35–40 revising: skipping the plan makes a paragraph lose direction, skipping revision leaves easy mistakes behind, and each costs half a band.

tips.title: Identify the question type first
tips.body: Read the question twice and underline the topic words and the instruction words separately — the type decides what goes in the conclusion. Argumentative: write the arguments of both sides and give an opinion in the conclusion. Narrative: write only what is asked; only a suggestion at the end. Combination: answer both questions, in separate paragraphs.

tips.title: Brainstorm before you pick a side
tips.body: Brainstorm on the question paper in two columns and do not stop until you have at least 3 points on one side; write weak ideas too, since selection comes later. Choose your side only after brainstorming: the side with the stronger arguments becomes yours, so the essay is automatically strong. In fact, the essay has already been made in the brainstorm.

tips.title: Introduction: general statement + thesis
tips.body: Write 2–3 sentences (40–55 words) with no argument yet: a general statement about the subject, then a thesis with your position, a hint of the main reason and, optionally, the other side with a softener. "This essay will discuss…" without your view is not a thesis, and do not start with a question.

tips.title: What never belongs in Task 2
tips.body: No memorised essays (the examiner recognises them at a glance), no contractions, slang or "etc.", and no headings, bullets or numbering — full sentences, full paragraphs. Don't use grammar or words you are not sure of: if not confident, write simple sentences and join them with linking words. One irrelevant sentence is forgiven, one irrelevant paragraph is not.

title: Task 2: body paragraphs, conclusion and essay types

tips.title: Topic sentence, explanation, example
tips.body: Every body paragraph has one idea: a topic sentence that states its main claim, 1–2 sentences of explanation if needed, and one concrete example (a country, an event, a common situation). Aim for 70–100 words per paragraph. A template is only a skeleton — fill it with content from your own topic.

tips.title: Emphasise your side, soften theirs
tips.body: In an argumentative essay use emphasisers (undoubtedly, clearly, the main, crucial) in your own points and softeners (may, some, arguably, it is sometimes claimed that) in the opposing points — every time. Present the other side and answer it: Although some shop owners may lose a little trade at first, a car-free centre undoubtedly attracts far more visitors in the long run.

tips.title: A short conclusion with your opinion
tips.body: In 1–2 sentences (30–45 words): a concluding connective plus your opinion in new words, and a suggestion if you like. Do not bring in a new argument, copy the thesis word for word, suddenly turn "balanced", end with a question, write "Thank you" or start with "Last but not least".

tips.title: Narrative: only what has been asked
tips.body: If the question is "What are the problems of tourism?", a paragraph on benefits is off-topic and costs a band. Use neutral language and give no opinion unless asked; a suggestion at the end is fine. In a problem–solution essay every solution must fix a problem you stated (cheap fast food → a tax or labelling, not "build more gyms").

tips.title: Combination: answer both questions
tips.body: Give each question its own body paragraph and roughly equal weight — not the first in detail and the second in one sentence. Mention both parts in the introduction and close both in the conclusion, restating your opinion for the argumentative part. It is one essay, with one introduction and one conclusion.
